text: Chapter two closes with the question that connects back to the versioning thread named back in lesson three: once a feature definition exists in a feature store, how do you track which version of it was used for a given model, and trace a problem backward from a bad prediction to the exact logic and data that produced it?

A feature view is code, and code changes — someone adjusts a rolling window from seven days to fourteen, or fixes a bug in a null-handling branch. If that change happens silently, every model trained before it and every model trained after it are implicitly using different features, even though both look like they're using the same name. The fix mirrors ordinary software versioning: feature definitions live in source control, so every change has a commit, an author, and a timestamp, just like application code.

Feast's own registry stores the currently-applied definitions, and feast apply is the command that pushes a change from source control into that registry. Run it after editing a feature view in Python, from the feature repo directory, and the registry now reflects exactly what's in source control — there's no path for a definition to change without a corresponding commit.

Lineage is the ability to answer, after the fact, three questions. Where did this feature's values actually come from — which raw data source. Which model versions were trained using this exact definition, and which are still on an older one. And when did this feature's logic last change, and what did it look like before. It's the forward-looking twin of skew detection — reconstructing history instead of comparing two live numbers.

Without this, answering "did a feature change underneath us" takes hours of manually diffing notebooks. With it, the answer is a commit log and a registry lookup — and in regulated industries, auditors expect exactly this kind of trace. That closes chapter two's look at feature stores. Up next, chapter three: experiment tracking and model registries, the next stop on a model's path to a production decision.
